Formatting and building custom tables

Source: vignettes/custom-tables.Rmd
custom-tables.Rmd

The table functions (sstable.baseline(), sstable.ae(), sstable.survcomp(), …) return either a finished flextable or, with flextable = FALSE, an sstable: a list with a character matrix table and a footer. This vignette shows how to turn sstables into report tables, how to edit them, and how to build a table of your own in the same style.

Function What it does
ss_flextable(), ss_huxtable() render an sstable as a flextable or huxtable
ft_sstheme(), ht_theme_kable(), ht_theme_markdown() apply the sstable look to any flextable or huxtable
sstable.baseline.edit() adds the header and footer to a baseline table you edited
ss_header(), ss_body(), ss_section(), ss_template(), ss_format() mark the rows of a hand-made table
print() prints an sstable matrix in the console 
library(C306)

The examples use baseline_data, a simulated two-arm trial bundled with the package.

bl <- baseline_data
bl$Arm <- factor(bl$Arm, levels = c("Sham procedure", "Intrathecal treatment"))
tab <- sstable.baseline(age + sex + bmi + ablettscore ~ Arm, data = bl)
names(tab)
#> [1] "table"  "footer"

Rendering: ss_flextable() and ss_huxtable()

ss_flextable() turns an sstable into a flextable with bold header rows, indented row groups and striped body rows. add_footer appends notes to the table’s own footer:

ss_flextable(tab, add_footer = "Data are simulated.")

ss_flextable(tab$table, footer = "A custom footer", bg = "#E8F0F8")

A custom footer

ss_huxtable() does the same with the huxtable package, which also prints to the console, LaTeX and Markdown. It needs huxtable, which is only suggested by C306:

ss_huxtable(tab, caption = "Baseline characteristics", caption_pos = "top")
Baseline characteristics

- II 60 (44%) 55 (41%)
- III 26 (19%) 27 (20%)
N is number of all patients, n is number of patients with non-missing value.
Summary statistic is absolute count (%) for categorical variable(s) and mean; median (Q1-Q3) for numeric variable(s).

Theming any table

The same look can be applied to tables not made by C306. ft_sstheme() themes a flextable:

ft_sstheme(flextable::flextable(head(bl[, c("usubjid", "age", "sex", "Arm")])))

ht_theme_markdown() (stripes) and ht_theme_kable() (borders, like knitr::kable()) theme a huxtable; header_rows says which rows are headers:

ht <- huxtable::as_hux(head(bl[, c("usubjid", "age", "sex", "Arm")]))
ht_theme_markdown(ht, header_rows = 1)
usubjid age sex Arm
SIM-001 63 F Intrathecal treatment
SIM-002 43 M Intrathecal treatment
SIM-003 33 M Sham procedure
SIM-004 18 F Intrathecal treatment
SIM-005 53 M Sham procedure
SIM-006 51 F Sham procedure 
ht_theme_kable(ht, header_rows = 1)
usubjid age sex Arm
SIM-001 63 F Intrathecal treatment
SIM-002 43 M Intrathecal treatment
SIM-003 33 M Sham procedure
SIM-004 18 F Intrathecal treatment
SIM-005 53 M Sham procedure
SIM-006 51 F Sham procedure

Printing in the console

An sstable matrix prints as a plain matrix, or, with huxtable installed and pretty = TRUE (the default, set by options(ss_pretty.print = )), as a formatted text table:

print(tab$table, pretty = FALSE)
#> $V1
#>  [1] ""               "Characteristic" "age"            "sex"           
#>  [5] "- F"            "- M"            "bmi"            "ablettscore"   
#>  [9] "- I"            "- II"           "- III"         
#> 
#> $V2
#>  [1] ""    "n"   "136" "136" ""    ""    "136" "136" ""    ""    ""   
#> 
#> $V3
#>  [1] "Intrathecal treatment (N=136)" "Summary statistic"            
#>  [3] "49; 49 (38-60)"                ""                             
#>  [5] "26 (19%)"                      "110 (81%)"                    
#>  [7] "21; 20 (18-23)"                ""                             
#>  [9] "50 (37%)"                      "60 (44%)"                     
#> [11] "26 (19%)"                     
#> 
#> $V4
#>  [1] ""    "n"   "135" "135" ""    ""    "135" "135" ""    ""    ""   
#> 
#> $V5
#>  [1] "Sham procedure (N=135)" "Summary statistic"      "49; 49 (38-58)"        
#>  [4] ""                       "27 (20%)"               "108 (80%)"             
#>  [7] "21; 21 (19-24)"         ""                       "53 (39%)"              
#> [10] "55 (41%)"               "27 (20%)"              
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "baseline_tbl" "ss_tbl"       "data.frame"

Editing a baseline table: sstable.baseline.edit()

To change the content of a baseline table before it is formatted, ask for the raw matrix with matrix.raw = TRUE, edit its cells, and pass it back to sstable.baseline.edit() with the same formula and data. It adds the header rows and the footer (footer adds your own notes). Keep the first column as it is: the function uses the variable names there to order the rows.

raw <- sstable.baseline(age + sex ~ Arm, data = bl, matrix.raw = TRUE)
raw
#>      [,1]  [,2]  [,3]             [,4]  [,5]            
#> [1,] "age" "136" "49; 49 (38-60)" "135" "49; 49 (38-58)"
#> [2,] "sex" "136" ""               "135" ""              
#> [3,] "- F" ""    "26 (19%)"       ""    "27 (20%)"      
#> [4,] "- M" ""    "110 (81%)"      ""    "108 (80%)"
raw[1, 3] <- paste0(raw[1, 3], "*")   # flag the age summary of the first arm
edited <- sstable.baseline.edit(raw, age + sex ~ Arm, data = bl,
                                footer = "* Illustrative flag added by hand.")
ss_flextable(edited)

To rename rows, set a label attribute on the variables before calling sstable.baseline() instead, as shown in vignette("C306_vignette_v6", package = "C306").

Building a table from scratch

Any character matrix can be rendered in the sstable style once its rows are marked as header, section (a row-group title) or body rows. The functions ss_header(), ss_section() and ss_body() do this one kind at a time:

m <- rbind(c("", "Sham procedure", "Intrathecal treatment"),
           c("Age, years", "50", "48"),
           c("Sex", "", ""),
           c("- Female", "30 (22%)", "29 (21%)"),
           c("- Male", "105 (78%)", "107 (79%)"))
m <- ss_header(m, 1)
m <- ss_body(m, c(2, 4, 5))
m <- ss_section(m, 3)
rownames(m)
#> [1] "header.1"  "body.1"    "section.1" "body.2"    "body.3"
ss_flextable(ss_format(m, .guess = FALSE))

Sham procedure

Intrathecal treatment

Age, years

50

48

Sex

- Female

30 (22%)

29 (21%)

- Male

105 (78%)

107 (79%)

ss_format() does it in one step. Give the rows of each kind, or let it guess: header rows come first, a section row has text only in its first column, and the rest are body rows. template ("baseline", "survcomp" or "ae", also set with ss_template()) chooses the layout rules:

m2 <- rbind(c("", "Sham procedure", "", "Intrathecal treatment", ""),
            c("Characteristic", "n", "Summary", "n", "Summary"),
            c("Age, years", "135", "50 (40-60)", "136", "48 (41-55)"),
            c("Sex", "", "", "", ""),
            c("- Female", "", "30 (22%)", "", "29 (21%)"))
f <- ss_format(m2)
rownames(f)
#> [1] "header.1"  "header.2"  "body.1"    "section.1" "body.2"
ss_flextable(f, footer = "Median (Q1-Q3) or n (%). Illustrative numbers.")

Tables made this way can be stacked with tables made by the package functions and with each other; see as_sstable() in vignette("regression", package = "C306") for assembling a table from header and body parts.
